See Kenneth W. Godfrey, “Making the Old Testament Live,” inA Symposium on the Old Testament(address to religious educators, Aug. 16–18, 1979), 111. InGenesis 50:1we learn that after Jacob’s death, “Joseph fell upon his father’s face, and wept upon him, and kissed him.”
See1 Chronicles 5:1–2. “The birthright then went to Joseph, who was the firstborn son of Jacob’s second wife, Rachel” (Guide to the Scriptures, “Israel,” Gospel Library).

The birthright son often inherited a double portion of the father’s possessions, which he was expected to use to help care for the physical needs of the family (seeDeuteronomy 21:17; see also Bradley R. Wilcox, “O Youth of the Noble Birthright,”Liahona, Nov. 2024, 94; Richard Neitzel Holzapfel and others,Jehovah and the World of the Old Testament: An Illustrated Reference for Latter-day Saints, 62).
SeeJoseph Smith Translation, Genesis 48:5–6, Gospel Library. See also Guide to the Scriptures, “Israel,” Gospel Library.

SeeGenesis 44:1–33. In the Old Testament, the Hebrew word translated as “servant” can also be translated as “slave.” The Hebrew word can denote either voluntary service or slavery (see Tremper Longman III and Mark L. Strauss,The Baker Expository Dictionary of Biblical Words[2023], entry 5650, page 998).

See Guide to the Scriptures, “Ephraim,” Gospel Library. Ludlow, “What Laws Governed the Inheritance of Birthright in the Old Testament?”Ensign, Sept. 1980, 53.
SeeGenesis 48:19–20. As with Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph, the birthright son in Abraham’s family was not always the eldest.

The interpretation given this passage by the … Church is one based on revelation to modern prophets, not on scholarly commentary. It was revealed to Joseph Smith that Shiloh is the Messiah [seeJoseph Smith Translation, Genesis 50:24, Gospel Library]” (“A Message to Judah from Joseph,”Ensign, Dec. 1976, 71).
